analysis.one_liner: Restores federal oversight of election changes in states with recent voting-rights violations and requires public notice of voting changes.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 111 cosponsors, including 18 Republicans, the bill never received a committee vote and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's 2013 Shelby County v. Holder decision struck down the Voting Rights Act's formula for deciding which states needed federal approval before changing election rules, this bill would have written a new formula based on recent conduct. States with five or more voting-rights violations in the previous 15 years, including one by the state itself, and counties or cities with three or more would again need federal approval before changing voting rules. The bill also required public notice of changes to voting procedures, polling place resources, and district lines; expanded federal election observers, including for bilingual-election enforcement; and let individual voters sue directly. It deliberately exempted voter photo-ID laws from triggering federal oversight.
analysis.who_benefits: Racial and language minority voters in states and localities with recent records of voting discrimination, who would regain advance federal review of election changes instead of having to challenge discriminatory rules after an election. All voters benefit from required public notice of changes to polling places, machines, poll workers, and district lines, since changes could no longer be made quietly weeks before an election.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minority voters in states with violation records

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new coverage formula keyed to actual conduct: a state is covered if it had five or more voting-rights violations in the previous 15 years including one by the state itself; a county, city, or school district is covered if it had three or more violations, or one or more plus persistently very low minority turnout.

Requires states and larger localities to give public notice within 48 hours of changing any voting procedure, and to publish polling place data, including the number of voting machines and poll workers assigned to each precinct, before an election.

Lets any aggrieved voter, not just the Attorney General, go to court for relief when their right to vote is denied, and directs courts to weigh the hardship on the voter against the hardship on the election official.
Expands the Attorney General's authority to send federal election observers, including to enforce bilingual election requirements after written complaints from residents or civic organizations.

analysis.who_pays: State and local election offices in jurisdictions with recent voting-rights violations would bear the cost of federal preclearance, public-notice requirements, and federal observers. States that enacted photo-ID laws would pay nothing, since the bill exempts photo ID from both the coverage formula and federal objection authority.

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out photo-identification requirements entirely: a voter-ID law cannot trigger coverage for a state or subdivision and cannot be the basis of a federal objection, leaving the most contested voting restriction of the era outside the bill's advance-review system.

The formula counts only violations already established in a final court judgment or a Justice Department objection, so a discriminatory change that has not yet been litigated does not bring a jurisdiction under coverage until after the fact.

Covered jurisdictions face real administrative burdens: pre-approval for election changes, ongoing public-notice obligations, and data reporting, which critics of preclearance view as unwarranted federal control of state election administration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was drafted as a narrower, evidence-based replacement for the old coverage formula: it reaches only jurisdictions with documented recent violations rather than the fixed 1960s-70s list, and the transparency requirements are inexpensive compliance work. The most serious defect is the complete photo-ID exemption, which leaves the highest-profile voting restriction of the period without advance review. For voters in covered jurisdictions, the protections would have outweighed the compliance burden; for the states affected, the burden was the point.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and sent to its Constitution and Civil Justice subcommittee in March 2015; the committee never held a markup or a vote, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 11, 2015 by Rep. Sensenbrenner with 19 original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Charlie Dent, Mike Fitzpatrick, and Chris Gibson.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
On March 16, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress.
The bill attracted 111 cosponsors, 93 Democrats and 18 Republicans, but no further action was ever taken on it, and the Congress expired without a House vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local jurisdictions with recent voting-rights violations are better off, since they remain free of the federal preclearance and notice requirements the bill would have imposed, as are the officeholders in those places who would have needed federal approval before changing election rules. Supporters of photo-ID laws also came out ahead in one sense: no comparable bill advanced, so no version of the oversight was restored at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Jurisdictions with violation records; photo-ID proponents

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-WI), former Chairman of the House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered bipartisan original cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill; it was sent to the Constitution and Civil Justice subcommittee and remained there.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan, with 93 of 188 Democrats and 18 of 247 Republicans cosigning, but no Republican-controlled committee ever took the bill up, and the House never voted.

industries.industry: State and local election officials in jurisdictions with recent voting-rights violations
industries.note: The bill would subject these jurisdictions to federal preclearance, 48-hour public-notice rules, polling resource disclosures, and possible federal observers. Their interest in changing election rules without advance federal review runs against the voters the bill protects.

industries.industry: State governments enacting voter photo-ID laws
industries.note: The bill expressly excludes photo-ID requirements from the coverage formula and from federal objection authority, so states could adopt and enforce ID laws without the advance review that would apply to other voting changes.
